lesson.title: The Price Tag on a Chemical Bond
lesson.summary: Bond energy measures how much energy it takes to break a bond, and that single number explains why some molecules sit around inert for millions of years while others react on contact.
lesson.body:
Every chemical bond has a price. Bond energy, also called bond dissociation energy, is the average energy required to break one mole of a particular type of bond in a gaseous molecule, producing separate gaseous atoms or fragments. Breaking a bond always costs energy, so the process is endothermic. Forming that same bond releases exactly that much energy back, an exothermic process called bond formation energy. The two are mirror images of each other: same magnitude, opposite sign. When chemists talk about a bond being strong, they usually mean its bond energy is large, so pulling it apart demands a large energy investment.

Bond energy is closely tied to bond order, the number of shared electron pairs between two atoms. As bond order increases, more electron density is packed between the two nuclei, pulling them closer together and holding them more tightly. A carbon to carbon single bond has a bond energy around 347 kilojoules per mole. A carbon to carbon double bond jumps to about 614 kilojoules per mole, and a carbon to carbon triple bond climbs to roughly 839 kilojoules per mole. More shared pairs mean a shorter, stronger bond, and a shorter, stronger bond means a larger bond energy. This is why triple bonds are consistently the hardest bonds to break in any molecule that contains them.

Nitrogen gas is the textbook case for why this matters outside the classroom. The nitrogen to nitrogen triple bond in N2 has a bond energy of about 945 kilojoules per mole, one of the strongest bonds found in any common molecule. That enormous bond energy is exactly why atmospheric nitrogen, despite making up nearly eighty percent of the air, is so chemically unreactive. Breaking it apart to make ammonia or nitrate fertilizer requires either industrial conditions of extreme heat and pressure, as in the Haber process, or the brief violence of a lightning bolt. Bond energy is not just an abstract number, it predicts real chemical behavior.

Chemists also use tables of average bond energies to estimate the enthalpy change of a reaction without running a calorimetry experiment. The logic follows directly from the endothermic and exothermic halves described above: energy must be put in to break the bonds in the reactants, and energy comes back out when new bonds form in the products. The estimate is written as the sum of bond energies broken minus the sum of bond energies formed. Because these are average values pulled from many different compounds, the result is an approximation, not an exact thermodynamic measurement, but it is often close enough to predict whether a reaction will release or absorb heat.

Consider the reaction of hydrogen gas with chlorine gas to form hydrogen chloride, H2 plus Cl2 giving two HCl. Breaking the bonds in the reactants costs one H to H bond, about 436 kilojoules per mole, plus one Cl to Cl bond, about 242 kilojoules per mole, for a total of 678 kilojoules per mole. Forming the products releases energy from two new H to Cl bonds, each about 431 kilojoules per mole, for a total of 862 kilojoules per mole. Subtracting gives 678 minus 862, or about negative 184 kilojoules per mole, meaning the reaction is exothermic. That estimate lines up closely with the experimentally measured value, which is a good demonstration of how useful bond energy tables can be for predicting reaction outcomes before any shape or geometry of the molecule even enters the picture.
